name: Cretan Extra Virgin Olive Oil
description: Cold-pressed olive oil from Cretan groves; among the highest polyphenol content of any EVOO globally.

name: Stamnagathi (Wild Chicory)
description: Bitter wild green foraged across Cretan hillsides; eaten boiled or in salads; rich in polyphenols and prebiotics.

name: Cretan Thyme Honey
description: Raw honey produced by bees foraging on wild thyme in the Cretan highlands; prized for antimicrobial and antioxidant properties.

name: Cretan Mountain Tea (Sideritis / Malotira)
description: Dried flowering tops of Sideritis syriaca brewed as herbal tea; known locally as malotira in Crete; consumed daily across rural Crete for centuries.

name: Cretan Sheep & Goat Dairy (Graviera & Anthotyros)
description: Traditional cheeses made from free-range sheep and goat milk; Graviera is a hard aged cheese; Anthotyros is a fresh whey cheese.

name: Purslane (Glistrida)
description: Succulent wild green harvested from Cretan fields and roadsides; one of the richest plant sources of omega-3 fatty acids.

name: Dittany of Crete (Origanum dictamnus)
description: Aromatic perennial herb endemic only to the cliffs and gorges of Crete; brewed as a delicate herbal infusion; used in Cretan folk medicine for over 2000 years; prized for digestive comfort and antimicrobial properties.

name: Cretan Carob (Ceratonia siliqua)
description: Pods of the carob tree cultivated in Crete for millennia; Crete produces approximately 75% of the global carob supply; eaten fresh or dried and made into a rich dark syrup; high in fibre, polyphenols, and D-pinitol.

name: Cretan Pomegranate (Punica granatum)
description: Deep-red seeded fruit cultivated in Crete for millennia; one of the most antioxidant-rich fruits studied in human clinical trials; peel and juice contain punicalagins with antioxidant capacity exceeding red wine and green tea; prized in Cretan culture as a symbol of fertility and health.

name: Cretan Artichoke (Cynara scolymus)
description: Edible thistle-like flower bud cultivated in Cretan fields since antiquity; rich in cynarin and chlorogenic acid which stimulate bile production and support liver health; a staple of traditional Cretan spring cooking and one of the oldest cultivated vegetables in the Mediterranean.

name: Olive Leaf Extract (Olea europaea leaf)
description: Dried leaves of the Cretan olive tree brewed as herbal tea or concentrated as extract; exceptionally rich in oleuropein — the bitter phenolic found at 10-20x higher concentrations in leaves than in olive oil; used in Cretan folk medicine as a natural antihypertensive remedy for centuries.

name: Cretan Barley & Paximadi (Hordeum vulgare)
description: Ancient Cretan grain baked into the iconic double-dried paximadi rusk — the traditional base of dakos; cultivated in Crete since the Minoan civilisation; exceptionally high in beta-glucan soluble fibre which earned an FDA health claim for cardiovascular disease risk reduction.

name: Cretan Garlic (Allium sativum)
description: Aromatic bulb cultivated in Cretan fields for over 4000 years; fundamental to traditional Cretan cuisine; each clove contains alliin which converts to allicin when crushed — the most extensively studied food-derived cardiovascular compound with 108 human RCTs documenting comprehensive benefits across lipid profiles, blood pressure, inflammation, and blood glucose.

name: Cretan Avocado (Persea americana)
description: Creamy subtropical fruit cultivated on the sun-facing coastal hillsides of western Crete; one of the few avocado-producing regions in Europe; exceptionally rich in oleic acid, beta-sitosterol, and potassium; Cretan avocados are prized for their dense buttery flesh and high monounsaturated fat content.

name: Cretan Table Olives (Olea europaea)
description: Traditional preserved olives from Cretan groves cured by natural brine, dry salt, or alkaline treatment; Crete produces some of the world's most prized table olives including the protected Kolymvari variety; contain free hydroxytyrosol at concentrations 8-fold higher than EVOO per gram of flesh; consumed throughout Crete as a staple meze since Minoan civilisation — the same polyphenols that make Cretan olive oil the most studied food in cardiology are even more concentrated here.

name: Cretan Sheep & Goat Probiotic Yoghurt
description: Traditionally strained yoghurt made from Cretan sheep and goat milk; richer in protein, calcium, and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) than standard cow's milk yoghurt; produced with live L. acidophilus and L. bulgaricus cultures that survive gastrointestinal transit; Cretan shepherds consumed fresh yoghurt daily as a dietary staple for centuries; the high fat content from pasture-raised animals and the probiotic cultures distinguish it from commercial yoghurt.

name: Cretan Savory (Satureja thymbra)
description: Aromatic perennial herb growing wild on Cretan hillsides and rocky coastal terrain; used in traditional Cretan cooking to season legumes, meat, and pickled olives; a close relative of Iranian savory (Satureja khuzestanica), the most clinically studied species in the genus; contains carvacrol and thymol as dominant phenolic compounds — the same bioactives found in dittany and oregano; known locally as throumbi and used for centuries in Cretan folk medicine.

name: Cretan Tomatoes (Solanum lycopersicum)
description: Sun-ripened tomatoes cultivated in Cretan fields; warm Cretan summers produce tomatoes with exceptionally high lycopene concentrations; fundamental to Cretan cuisine in dakos, stews, and salads; cooking tomatoes in olive oil dramatically increases lycopene bioavailability — lycopene is fat-soluble and the traditional Cretan pairing of cooked tomatoes with EVOO maximises absorption; one of the most replicated diet-cardiovascular pairings in Mediterranean nutrition science.

name: Cretan Onions (Allium cepa)
description: Pungent bulb cultivated extensively across Cretan fields and fundamental to traditional cuisine as the flavour base of virtually every Cretan dish; dry outer skin layers contain the highest quercetin concentrations of any commonly consumed vegetable (300-500 mg/kg fresh weight); red and yellow varieties both consumed raw in horiatiki salads and cooked in stews; quercetin glucoside — the form in onions — is one of the most bioavailable dietary flavonols.

name: Cretan Oregano (Origanum vulgare)
description: Intensely aromatic wild herb growing abundantly across Cretan hillsides; considered among the finest dried oregano in the world due to exceptionally high essential oil concentrations; used universally in Cretan cooking on salads, grilled meats, and fish; belongs to the same Origanum genus as Dittany of Crete and shares its dominant bioactive compounds carvacrol and rosmarinic acid; Cretan rigani contains among the highest documented rosmarinic acid levels of any dried herb.

name: Cretan Wine Vinegar
description: Traditional vinegar produced by double fermentation of local Cretan grape varieties including Vidiano, Vilana, and Mandilari; acetic acid content (4-8%) is the primary bioactive responsible for documented glycaemic and metabolic benefits; Cretan wine vinegar is used in traditional salad dressings and as a condiment; grape-derived polyphenols including resveratrol and quercetin partially survive the fermentation process into the final vinegar.

name: Cretan Fennel (Foeniculum vulgare)
description: Tall aromatic perennial growing wild across Cretan roadsides, hillsides, and coastal areas; all parts used in Cretan cooking — bulb in salads and braised dishes, fronds in hortopita (herb pies), seeds as digestive herb tea; the primary bioactive trans-anethole relaxes gastrointestinal smooth muscle and accounts for the traditional use as a post-meal digestive herb; Crete has one of the richest wild fennel populations in the Mediterranean.

name: Cretan Mastic (Pistacia lentiscus)
description: Aromatic resin tapped from the mastic shrub (Pistacia lentiscus var. chia) — cultivated for over 2500 years in the Eastern Mediterranean including Crete; chewed traditionally as a digestive aid and breath freshener, used in pastries, liqueurs, and the Cretan herbal infusion mastichi; contains triterpenic acids (masticadienonic acid, isomasticadienonic acid) and the volatile alpha-pinene that drive its demonstrated gastrointestinal and antimicrobial effects.

name: Cretan Capers (Capparis spinosa)
description: Wild caper buds and fruit foraged from Cretan coastal cliffs and rocky terrain where the Capparis spinosa shrub thrives in extreme heat and salt spray; salt-cured or vinegar-brined and used in salads, fish dishes, and meze; exceptionally rich in quercetin and rutin — among the highest plant concentrations documented — and traditionally used in Mediterranean folk medicine for diabetes and metabolic complaints; modern RCTs in T2DM patients confirm the traditional use.

name: Cretan Walnuts (Juglans regia)
description: Walnut trees cultivated across the cooler highland villages of Crete since antiquity; the kernel is exceptionally rich in alpha-linolenic acid (plant omega-3), gamma-tocopherol, ellagic acid, and dietary melatonin; consumed whole, ground into stuffings, and as the base of traditional preserves like karydaki (walnut sweet); one of the most extensively studied nuts in cardiovascular nutrition — featured as one of the two intervention arms of the landmark PREDIMED trial showing reduced cardiovascular events.

name: Cretan Almonds (Prunus dulcis)
description: Almond trees cultivated extensively in Cretan groves alongside olive trees; the kernel is the richest plant source of alpha-tocopherol (vitamin E) among commonly consumed nuts, dominated by oleic acid (the same MUFA as EVOO); used in soumada (the traditional Cretan almond drink), in pastries like amygdalota, and as a meze; extensively studied — multiple meta-analyses of RCTs confirm consistent reductions in total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and body weight without adverse effects.

name: Cretan Sage (Salvia fruticosa)
description: Greek sage — Salvia fruticosa, also known as Salvia triloba — is the dominant Salvia species across the Cretan hillsides and one of the most widely consumed traditional herbal teas in Greece; brewed as faskomilo and drunk for centuries for memory and digestive support; chemotype is dominated by 1,8-cineole (eucalyptol), beta-thujone, and rosmarinic acid — distinct from Northern European Salvia officinalis; the Salvia genus has clinical trials demonstrating acute and chronic cognitive enhancement in humans, validating the Cretan tradition of drinking sage tea for mental clarity.

name: Cretan Legumes (Revithia & Fakes)
description: Ancient staples of the Cretan table since Minoan times — revithia (chickpeas) and fakes (lentils) form the backbone of iconic slow-cooked Cretan soups; rich in soluble fibre, resistant starch, and plant protein; among the most nutrient-dense and low-glycaemic foods in the Mediterranean diet.

name: Cretan Sea Fennel (Kritamo)
description: Wild aromatic halophyte that grows on the rocky cliffsides and coves of Crete; harvested for millennia and traditionally pickled or used fresh in mezze; rich in chlorogenic acid, terpenoids, and omega-3 and omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids; one of the most distinctive wild greens in the Cretan foraging tradition.

name: Cretan Citrus (Lemon & Orange)
description: Lemons and oranges cultivated throughout Crete — especially in the groves of the Chania region — for centuries; the peel and juice are the primary source of hesperidin, the most studied citrus flavanone; integral to Cretan cooking, used in dressings, marinades, and the iconic avgolemono sauce.

name: Cretan Figs (Syka)
description: One of the oldest cultivated fruits in Crete — both fresh and sundried — mentioned in Minoan frescoes and central to the traditional Cretan diet; the skin and flesh are rich in anthocyanins, rutin, chlorogenic acid, and dietary fibre; dried Cretan figs remain a seasonal staple eaten with cheese and walnuts.

name: Cretan Snails (Hohlioi)
description: One of Crete's most iconic wild foods — gathered from thyme-scented hillsides after the first autumn rains and fried in olive oil with rosemary and salt in the legendary dish hohlioi boubouristi; the flesh of Helix aspersa is lean (~77 kcal per 100g), rich in complete protein with all essential amino acids, and has a favourable omega-3 to omega-6 fatty acid ratio with predominantly unsaturated fats.
